intro: No verified study gives a standard SBAR shift report time per patient. The fastest honest answer is the number your own unit produces, so time your report across several shifts before you change anything. This page covers how to time it on a Mac, what slow handoffs cost, why report runs long, and fixes that cost nothing.
tldr: No verified study gives a standard SBAR shift report time per patient.
Time your own report across several shifts. Then change one thing at a time.
The cost shows up as late finishes, extra charting, and details that get lost.
A fixed order, a one-line summary, and questions per patient cut the wandering.
Lazur helps with dictation and explanations, but your employer's patient data rules come first.

blocks.text: How long SBAR shift report takes per patient

The short answer is that the sources I checked give no standard number. I could not find a verified study that times SBAR per patient at shift change. That means there is no official figure to copy onto your unit. The number you need is the one your own shift produces, and a timer plus a few shifts of notes will get it.

The closest study I could open ran on one pediatric unit with 28 full-time RNs. Nurses moved report from the nurses' station to the bedside. Their rating that shift report finishes in a reasonable time rose from 2.14 to 4.16 on a 5-point scale. The authors did not measure how long report took. A rating shows how people felt, not how many minutes passed. Treat it as a clue, not a benchmark.

blocks.title: Do not copy another unit's number
blocks.text: A per-patient time depends on patient count, acuity, where report happens, and how your unit orders the talk. A number from a different unit or hospital can mislead you. Measure your own, then compare your unit against itself over time.
How to time your own SBAR report on a Mac

You need a timer, a notes app, and a shift where you give report. Use a timer on your phone, or ask Lazur to set one by voice. Do not write patient names in the log. Write the time, the patient count, and a short reason for any long patient instead.

items: Start the timer when you say the first word of the first patient.
Stop it when the last patient's questions are answered and the talk ends.
Write the total time next to the number of patients you reported on.
Divide the total by the patient count. That is your average per patient.
Note any patient who ran long and why, such as a new order or a rapid response.
Repeat across several shifts so one odd night does not set your number.

blocks.text: Use the log to find the pattern, not only the average. Say most patients take a short time each, and a few take far longer. The average hides that. Split the log into routine patients and complex ones. The complex ones usually show where the time goes.

Keep the log in a file your employer allows you to use. In Notes or Word, press ⌘F to find a flagged patient or a reason word such as order. Delete any detail that could identify a patient before you save the file.
What slow SBAR shift report costs you

The price of a slow handoff is mostly paid after you clock out. Late finishes, extra charting, and details that surface after the other nurse leaves all land on you or the next shift. The turnover data below shows what staffing strain costs hospitals. It does not prove that handoff time causes turnover, so read it as context.

The numbers are large. NSI's 2026 report, as summarized by Becker's, puts the average cost per staff RN turnover at $60,090 for 2025. National average staff RN turnover reached 17.6% that year, up 1.2 points. NCSBN's 2024 workforce study found that 40% of RNs planned to leave the profession within 5 years.

blocks.text: Specialty matters too. Becker's reports 2025 RN turnover of 22.5% in behavioral health and 19.5% in telemetry. If you work on one of those units, check whether your report carries more monitoring data per patient. That load is worth timing on its own.

A slow report also shapes how you feel about the job. Nurses who dread report often skip the questions. That can turn into a safety cost, not just a time cost. A shorter, more predictable talk is the place to start.
Why SBAR runs long at shift change

The sources I checked do not measure the causes of slow handoffs. The patterns below come from how report usually runs on busy units. Treat them as things to check on your own unit. Do not treat them as proven causes.

items: Report starts before the outgoing nurse has finished the last task.
Everyone talks at once at the station, so details get repeated.
There is no fixed order, so the talk jumps between background and today's plan.
Background gets read in full, even for patients who are stable.
Questions wait until the end, when everyone wants to leave.
Phones, call lights, and people walking in restart the talk.

blocks.text: Location is a cause you can change. Report at the nurses' station means people talk over each other, and the outgoing nurse gets pulled away. The single pediatric study moved report to the bedside and reported better ratings, though it did not measure time. Bedside report needs an agreed policy and a quiet room. Raise it with your unit leader rather than starting it alone.
Fixes you can use without buying anything

These fixes cost nothing, and most need only your unit's agreement. Pick one. Run it for several shifts, then time it again with the same method as before. If the number does not move, drop that fix and try the next one.

items: Keep one fixed order: situation, background, assessment, recommendation, every time.
Open each patient with a single line that names the reason for the report.
Give stable patients a short report and save the longer talk for changes.
Hold questions until the end of each patient, not the end of the whole round.
Write the to-do items down, one short list per patient, and read them back.
Use a bedside check when your unit allows it, so the talk matches the patient.

blocks.text: Write the SBAR once, then reuse the structure

A template helps when it holds structure, not patient data. In Word on your Mac, open a blank document and add a heading for each SBAR part. Then choose File > Save As, and pick Word Template in the format list. Save it to a folder your employer allows.

Keep the template blank. A saved note with a patient's name in it is a privacy problem, and the template repeats that problem every time you open it. Check your employer's rule on where drafts can live before you save anything.
A worked example of a short SBAR at the bedside

Here is an example with no real patient details. A patient had surgery this morning and now reports new pain. The drain output changed at the last check. Situation: pain is not controlled, and the drain output has changed. Background: surgery this morning, with a pain plan already written.

Assessment: pain is higher than at the last check, and the drain output looks different. Recommendation: call for a pain review and ask for the drain output to be measured at the next check. The talk stays short because each part says one thing. The next nurse knows what to watch and what to ask.
Notice what is missing. There are no lab values, no full medication list, and no history read aloud. Those belong in the chart. Read the chart after report, and add the detail there.
Mistakes people make with SBAR at shift change

items: Reading the whole chart aloud instead of the changes.
Skipping the recommendation, so the next nurse has to guess what to do.
Giving report in a noisy hallway, then repeating it later at the bedside.
Treating SBAR as a checklist instead of a way to describe what changed.
Timing the report once and assuming the number holds for good.
Keeping a shared template that holds real patient data on a personal device.

blocks.text: The most common mistake is timing the report once and assuming it holds. Staffing, acuity, and habits change. Time again after a change, then decide what to keep.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on your screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a button is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

Dictation fits this problem best. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. You can dictate a draft SBAR into Word, Outlook, or Google Docs, then edit it yourself. Snippets, a personal dictionary, and clipboard slots help when you say the same phrases each shift.

Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. It is not a plugin or add-in for Word, Outlook, Chrome, or any charting system. It has no partnership with any app maker, so do not expect it to pull data from your electronic record.
Privacy and your employer's rules for patient data

blocks.title: Patient data comes first
blocks.text: Follow your employer's rules on patient data before you use any AI tool. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Keep patient names, birth dates, and record numbers off the screen while you hold the shortcut.

If your hospital bans AI tools near patient data, follow that rule. Ask Lazur for general help with no patient details, such as how to lay out a template or what a clear recommendation sounds like. Type the patient-specific part yourself, in your approved system.
Epic and hospital tools on a Mac

Many hospitals run clinical tools that were built for other devices. The App Store listing for Epic Canto shows it for iPad only, with iPadOS 18.0 or later and version 11.9.3. Your organization has to license it. Check with your IT team before you assume a Mac version exists, and do not install anything from a link a coworker sends.
What to do this week

Start with the timing log, which needs no new tools. If your report lives in Word, read [Word for nurses on Mac](/for/nurses/word) for template ideas. If you check orders or results in a browser, [Chrome for nurses on Mac](/for/nurses/chrome) covers tabs and shortcuts. For shift emails, see [Outlook for nurses on Mac](/for/nurses/outlook).
When the week ends, compare the new log with the old one. Look for the patients that still run long, and fix those first. A calm, repeatable report beats a fast one that skips the recommendation.

faq.question: How long should SBAR shift report take per patient?
faq.answer: No verified source gives a standard number. The pediatric study I checked measured how nurses felt about report time, not minutes. Time your own report across several shifts with a timer, then use your average as your baseline.

faq.question: Is there an official time limit for SBAR handoff?
faq.answer: I could not open the Joint Commission's handoff guidance, so I cannot confirm an official time limit. Check your hospital's handoff policy, and ask your nurse educator which current guidance applies to your unit.

faq.question: Does SBAR take longer than an unstructured report?
faq.answer: The sources I checked do not compare the two for time. Test it on your unit. Time a shift with your usual talk, then a shift with a fixed order, and compare the averages.

faq.question: Can Lazur time my shift report?
faq.answer: Lazur sets timers by voice, so you can start one without leaving your work. It does not decide when report starts or ends. You still start the timer and stop it when the talk is done.

faq.question: Can I dictate SBAR notes with Lazur?
faq.answer: Yes. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Follow your employer's rules on patient data first, and keep names and record numbers out of the dictation unless your employer allows it.

faq.question: Does Lazur connect to Epic or our electronic health record?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is not a plugin or add-in for any app, and it has no partnership with any app maker. It does not click buttons or pull records from your electronic health record.

faq.question: Is Lazur available on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available.

faq.question: How much does Lazur cost after the trial?
faq.answer: The Pro plan is $18/month, or $15/month billed annually, with 250 AI actions. Power is $120/month, or $96/month billed annually, with 1,000 AI actions. Dictation is unlimited on both. The 3-day Pro trial needs no credit card. Check [pricing](/pricing) for the current terms.

faq.question: What if my hospital bans AI tools?
faq.answer: Then follow that rule. Use your approved tools for anything about patients. You can still use the timing method, the fixed order, and the blank template on this page with no AI at all.

costs.title: Time after clock-out
costs.text: Report that runs past the end of your shift adds time you did not plan for. It can mean overtime, or a late exit with patients still on your mind. Compare your clock-out time with the time report started, for one week, and you will see the gap.

costs.title: Extra charting after report
costs.text: Details that should be said at the bedside often show up later as notes you write after the shift. Count the notes you add in the hour after report. If the number is high, the handoff may be missing details the chart needs.

costs.title: Missed details and callbacks
costs.text: A question that waits until the end of the round can be answered late, or not at all. Callbacks from the next shift take time and can delay care. Track the calls you get in the first hour after report and note what they were about.

costs.title: Staff strain and turnover risk
costs.text: Nurses who dread report often leave the talk tired and short on time. NCSBN's 2024 study found 40% of RNs planned to leave within 5 years. The study does not measure handoff, so treat any link to report as a guess to test on your unit.

costs.title: Patient safety risk
costs.text: When report runs long or skips the recommendation, the next nurse may not know what to watch. In the one pediatric study I checked, nurses rated 'promptly identifying changes in patient status' from 1.9 to 4.21 after bedside handoff. That is a staff rating, not a safety outcome.

causes.title: Report starts at the nurses' station
causes.text: At the station, people talk over each other, and the outgoing nurse gets pulled toward the next task. Details get repeated, and the talk loses its thread. The sources I checked did not measure this, so test it by timing one bedside report against one station report.

causes.title: No fixed order
causes.text: When each nurse starts in a different place, the listener cannot predict where the important part will be. The talk jumps between background and today's plan. Listeners then miss the change they most needed to hear.

causes.title: Background read in full
causes.text: Long background sections eat most of the time, even for patients who are stable. The change is often a single line, but it gets buried in history. Read the history from the chart, and say only the parts that bear on the next hours.

causes.title: Questions held until the end
causes.text: When questions wait until the whole round is over, everyone wants to leave, and the answers come fast or not at all. Questions about one patient fade by the time the talk reaches the next one. That is why the same question often comes back later.

causes.title: Interruptions during the talk
causes.text: Phones, call lights, and people walking in restart the talk. Each restart means repeating a line or losing the thread. A quiet space and a clear start line reduce the restarts, but only if the unit agrees to protect them.

causes.title: Uneven patient load
causes.text: Nurses with more patients, or with more unstable ones, report on more ground in the same slot. The sources I checked did not measure this for shift report. Check it with your own log by splitting the times by patient count and acuity.

fixes.title: Time one shift first
fixes.text: Before you change the report, time it once with the method above. A baseline tells you whether a fix worked. Without one, you are guessing, and a fix that feels faster may not be faster at all.

fixes.title: Lock the order
fixes.text: Use the same four SBAR parts in the same sequence every time. The listener knows where to look for the change. Write the order on a card at the station if your unit allows it, then practice it for a week.

fixes.title: Lead with the reason
fixes.text: Open each patient with one line that says why this patient matters now, such as a new order or a change in pain. The rest of the talk fills in that line. Listeners stop wandering when they know the point early.

fixes.title: Shorten the stable patients
fixes.text: Give stable patients a short report, and save the longer talk for patients with changes or new orders. This is a sorting habit, and it takes a few shifts to build. Agree on what counts as stable with your unit so the rule is shared.

fixes.title: Hold questions for each patient
fixes.text: Ask questions after each patient, not after the whole round. A question about one patient gets answered while that patient is still fresh. It also keeps the next patient from blurring into the last one.

fixes.title: Write the to-do list down
fixes.text: Keep one short list per patient with the next action, the time, and the owner. Read it back before the talk ends. A written list catches what a spoken talk drops, and the next nurse can check it at a glance.

fixes.title: Keep the template free of patient data
fixes.text: Use a blank SBAR template with headings only. Fill it in with patient details in your approved system, then speak from it. This keeps the structure consistent without storing patient data in a personal file.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Time one shift
plan.text: Start a timer at the first patient and stop it when the talk ends. Write the total time and the patient count in a Notes file. Do not add patient names or record numbers to the log.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Mark the long patients
plan.text: Note which patients ran long and why. Look for patterns such as new orders, fresh admissions, or interruptions. Circle the most common reason in the log.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Pick one fix
plan.text: Choose one fix from this page. Build a blank SBAR template in Word with headings only, and use the same four parts in the same order every time.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Run the fix
plan.text: Use the fix at report. Ask a colleague to tell you when the talk drifts off the order. Keep the log going so you can compare later.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Review with your unit
plan.text: Share the averages with your unit leader. Ask whether the fix can become a unit habit. Follow your employer's rules on what you share and with whom.

plan.label: Week 2
plan.title: Time it again
plan.text: Use the same timing method for several shifts. Compare the new average and the long-patient notes with your first log. Keep the fix if it helped, and drop it if it did not.
